Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Glam Estate Group, established in 2024, focuses on creating fewer but better projects, with a philosophy rooted in human-centric design and timeless quality. The Accenta Phuket is a boutique development situated on the southern side of the Laem Sai peninsular that separates Karon and Kata beaches, both of which an easy two minutes walk away.

Sea views over Kata bay are available from all of 12 one-bedroom and 4 three-bedroom apartments which make up the project. This development is both visually stunning and innovative. Much time and thought has been given to the design concept, and laid out so that the best views were obtained from any balcony or terrace. Decorative columns adorn the rear entrance of the building with a spectacular spiral staircase accessing the upper floors. A beautifully landscaped lower terrace with 18m lap pool add to The Accenta’s unique serene ambience. The interior is of a modern tropical design, with a contemporary Japanese influence, and is finished to a very high standard using the finest quality materials.

The apartments are due for completion by mid-2006. Once finished they will be fully managed, with services including 24 hour security, maids and a rental facility for those wishing a return on their investment.

Apartment owners will enjoy access to facilities at the neighbouring Aspasia Phuket Resort and Spa, where the facilities include the highly acclaimed Malina’s Bistro and bakery and the Columns Restaurant, a gymnasium and one of the island’s top rated spas.

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Karon Beach Road promenade with restaurants and bars; Karon Plaza shopping strip; Karon Temple Market (Tuesdays and Fridays) for Thai street food and clothing; Big C Karon and Karon Bazaar for groceries; Kata Centre and Beach Road 5 minutes south for additional restaurants and shopping; The Movenpick Karon and Hilton Arcadia hotel hubs.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Kamala Beach Road with cafes and dive shops; Cafe del Mar Phuket area (beachfront events and dining); Plaza del Mar boutique mall; Kamala Fresh Market on the main road; Cherngtalay corridor reachable in 10 minutes north.

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Chalong Circle with banks, Makro, Tesco Lotus and visa offices; Chalong Pier for island boats and seafood; Big Buddha access road; Villa Market in Chalong; Wat Chalong temple and surrounding local food strip; Friday Phuket Town night market 15 minutes north.

Nai Yang sits inside Sirinat National Park, just south of Mai Khao and a few minutes north of the airport. The bay is a long shallow arc with calm water in the dry season and proper Andaman swell in green season, which makes it one of the few west coast spots where local surfers actually gather. The village strip is small but real: a row of seafood restaurants facing the beach under the casuarina trees, a few dive shops, two yoga studios, a daily night market that sets up on the inland road and a small cluster of guesthouses. That mix gives Nai Yang a character that Mai Khao lacks. There is a village to walk to in the evening, a community of long-stay foreign residents who actually use it, and prices for both rentals and groceries are noticeably softer than down at Bang Tao. The resident expat profile leans toward families, retirees and remote workers who decided that proximity to the airport and a quieter beach mattered more than walking distance to Boat Avenue. Schools are 20 to 25 minutes south, hospitals are 30 minutes, and a car or scooter is essential. The Slate and Marriott resorts anchor the upper end of the dining scene, and the Carpe Diem and Coco Beach groups handle casual sunset crowds. Nai Yang rewards buyers who want a village feel without leaving the west coast.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (16 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (15 km, public, major trauma centre).

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

The villas feature sleek architecture and spacious interiors filled with natural light and premium finishes. The well-planned layout includes two expansive master bedrooms with en-suite bathrooms, ensuring a luxurious living experience for every resident. The interiors showcase high-quality materials and sophisticated details, creating an atmosphere of exquisite style.

Perfect for both relaxation and entertainment, each villa offers elegant living spaces, a private pool, and beautifully landscaped gardens that provide a serene tropical retreat. Advanced smart home systems enhance convenience and security, making daily living effortless.

With its prime location near Kata Beach and its luxurious amenities, Amber offers the perfect blend of elegance, comfort, and ideal location. Whether you’re looking for a tranquil getaway or a space to entertain, these villas deliver an exceptional living experience for those who appreciate the best in contemporary tropical living.

Kata sits on the southwest coast, two bays south of Patong and one north of Nai Harn. The area is built around two beaches, Kata Yai and the smaller Kata Noi, both with cleaner sand and calmer water than Patong, plus a reliable surf break from May to October that keeps a small but committed long-stay surf community on the island year round. The foreign population here splits into three groups: surf and dive instructors who came on a season and stayed, retirees who chose Kata over Rawai for direct beach access, and remote workers who rent condos in Kata Hills for the views. Day to day life is walkable along Kata Beach Road and Patak Road, with bakeries, Thai kitchens, two small supermarkets and a steady rotation of cafes opening and closing each season. Nightlife is low key compared to Patong: a handful of bars, the Ska Bar sundowner spot under the banyan tree, and the weekend Kata Night Market for street food. Schools require a car, with Kajonkiet the closest international option and the Phuket Town cluster reachable in 25 to 30 minutes. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the Chalong side of the hill. The trade-offs are real high season traffic on the Patak hill road and limited supermarket options on site, but Kata works well for buyers who want a proper beach lifestyle without Patong density.

Kata Beach Road with cafes, dive shops and surf rentals; Kata Night Market (weekends) on Patak Road; Karon Plaza shopping strip (3 km north); Big C and Tesco Lotus in Chalong (10 km east) for full grocery runs.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Nai Yang sits inside Sirinat National Park, just south of Mai Khao and a few minutes north of the airport. The bay is a long shallow arc with calm water in the dry season and proper Andaman swell in green season, which makes it one of the few west coast spots where local surfers actually gather. The village strip is small but real: a row of seafood restaurants facing the beach under the casuarina trees, a few dive shops, two yoga studios, a daily night market that sets up on the inland road and a small cluster of guesthouses. That mix gives Nai Yang a character that Mai Khao lacks. There is a village to walk to in the evening, a community of long-stay foreign residents who actually use it, and prices for both rentals and groceries are noticeably softer than down at Bang Tao. The resident expat profile leans toward families, retirees and remote workers who decided that proximity to the airport and a quieter beach mattered more than walking distance to Boat Avenue. Schools are 20 to 25 minutes south, hospitals are 30 minutes, and a car or scooter is essential. Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

That mix gives Nai Yang a character that Mai Khao lacks. There is a village to walk to in the evening, a community of long-stay foreign residents who actually use it, and prices for both rentals and groceries are noticeably softer than down at Bang Tao. Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Kamala Beach Road with cafes and dive shops; Cafe del Mar Phuket area (beachfront events and dining); Plaza del Mar boutique mall; Kamala Fresh Market on the main road; Cherngtalay corridor reachable in 10 minutes north.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

Kata sits on the southwest coast, two bays south of Patong and one north of Nai Harn. The area is built around two beaches, Kata Yai and the smaller Kata Noi, both with cleaner sand and calmer water than Patong, plus a reliable surf break from May to October that keeps a small but committed long-stay surf community on the island year round. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the Chalong side of the hill. The trade-offs are real high season traffic on the Patak hill road and limited supermarket options on site, but Kata works well for buyers who want a proper beach lifestyle without Patong density.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

The vibrant world famous Patong Beach facing the west with all its activities and sun loungers, the rather northern palm-fringed Tri Trang Beach, Merlin Beach and Freedom Beach facing south, and Paradise Beach at the end of the peninsula. It is also just 15 minutes' walk from the beach, Jungceylon Shopping Center and the famous Bangla Road nightlife, which is full of bars. discos, restaurants, clubs and entertainment venues. There is absolutely everything from beach activities in Patong: jet skis, bananas, parachutes, kayak, paddle and surfboard rental. There are also volleyball nets on the beach for fans of this team game. Bangla is home to the largest discotheque in Phuket - Illuzion. For lovers of club life, there are two floors, a large dance floor and VIP rooms. The nightclub features famous international DJs and great shows. Worldwide restaurants including the popular Hard Rock Cafe. There are Thai food stalls and fruit stalls, fresh juices and fresh juices, massage parlours, convenience stores and Seven-Eleven shops. A little further in the depths of Patong, the Junqceylon shopping center is open, with stores of both national Thai and world brands. On its territory there is also a department store "Robinson" and "Big C". And in front of Junqceylon, next to Bangla Road, a new Central Festival was opened.

A great choice to explore Phuket or just relax and recharge on vacation.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Baan Bua is one of the largest luxury residences in the south of Phuket. The project consists of 59 luxury Thai-Balinese style villas, ranging from 150 m2, each with 3 to 5 bedrooms. The whole project is made in the same style. Several villa layouts depending on the number of bedrooms. The main building is U-shaped, in which there is a living room combined with a kitchen, several bedrooms isolated from each other with their own bathrooms. In the center there is a large swimming pool and a gazebo for relaxation. Each villa has its own covered parking. The villas are fenced off from each other and are completely private. The project is literally immersed in tropical greenery on the territory of the complex there is a lake, some of the villas have a private exit to it

The Baan Bua project is a small, well-kept town with green paths for hiking and cycling. The project is guarded around the clock, the office of the service company is also located here.

One of the best beaches - Nai Harn is located within one kilometre from the project. The beach is popular with families with children and expats, so you will not find a large crowd of tourists here. A stone's throw from the beach, there is a freshwater lake and an observation deck with windmills. Nai Harn Beach is popular with families with children, as well as with long-term guests of the island. It is comfortable to spend your vacation here, because Nearby there are many restaurants like European. and national Thai cuisine. There are also offices with transport rental and excursion services. For a long stay on Nai Harn, it is comfortable to live for families with children - there are international and Thai kindergartens, international and Russian schools nearby. The way from Nai Harn to the popular children's playground "Rawai Park" will take 5 minutes by car or bike.

Also Nai Harn is often chosen for yoga tours or sports campings. At Nai Harn and in the neighbouring Rawai district, there are gyms, specialised rings for Thai boxing and workout grounds. A 7-10 minute drive is a hypermarket Makro, a supermarket with European products Villa Market, a fish market.

The complex is ideal for absolutely everyone. The large size of the villas attracts large families with children. The location of the villas provides privacy, the peculiarity of the layout with private, non-contiguous bedrooms is popular with large campaigns from several families.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Nai Harn Beach Road and lagoon park; Rawai seafront (5 minutes east) for fresh seafood and weekly markets; Wyndham Grand Nai Harn and The Nai Harn hotel hubs for dining and gym access; Chalong Circle (10 km northeast) for Makro and visa offices.

Mission Hospital Phuket (14 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (18 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (17 km, public, major trauma centre).

The complex is located right on the shore of the beautiful deserted Beach natai surrounded by five-star hotels. The project includes six three-storey buildings and three five-storey buildings - a total of 206 apartments ranging from 59 to 264 sq.m. The complex has 1 bedroom apartments with an area of 68 m2 and 2 bedrooms, ranging from 90 m2. Each apartment is equipped with a TV with satellite channels, an equipped kitchen with a microwave and a refrigerator, a washing machine and a bathroom with a shower.

On-site parking for 100 cars, an excellent garden, swimming pool, fitness room, internet and 24-hour video surveillance. Condominium offers a professional concierge service for owners. From the very first moment you arrive in Phuket, you will have access to services such as airport pick-up (15 minutes from the airport), babysitting and food delivery directly to your door. It offers apartments with free Wi-Fi, air conditioning and a garden. This beachfront complex has access to a terrace. Active guests can go cycling in the surrounding area or rent a car.

Baan Mai Khao Beach Residence is located on Mai Khao Beach, 300 metres from Mai Khao Beach and 11 km from Splash Jungle Water Park. The complex is located right on the shore surrounded by five-star hotels and is estimated at 28 billion baht. Famous hotels in the vicinity include JW Marriott Phuket Resort and Spa, Anantara Phuket Resort and Spa, Sala Phuket and Renaissance Phuket Resort and Spa.

The complex is ideal for couples with children. If you want to take a break from the hustle and bustle of the bustling city and enjoy nature and the sea - this will be a good choice!

Mai Khao is the longest beach on Phuket, an 11 kilometre stretch on the very north end of the island, mostly protected as part of Sirinat National Park. Because of that protection, the coastline is almost free of the usual shophouse strip. Development here means a thin line of large resorts, JW Marriott, Anantara, Renaissance, SALA, Marriott Vacation Club, set behind a wide casuarina belt, with very little outside them. Foreign residents in Mai Khao are typically owners inside one of the branded residences attached to those resorts, or buyers in the small condo and villa clusters that sit just inland of the highway. The community is small, older and quiet, with a strong share of European and Asian second-home owners who use the property a few months a year. The main practical advantage of living here is the airport, which is six to ten minutes by car, so travel-heavy buyers and pilots actually consider it the best base on the island. The trade-off is the rest of the infrastructure. There is no real town strip, no walking grocery, and a trip to the international schools or major hospital is a 25 minute drive south. The beach itself is fantastic: empty most of the year, with sea turtles still nesting in season, and a noticeable absence of jet skis.

Turtle Village shopping plaza next to JW Marriott (cafes, mini-mart, small boutiques); Anantara Mai Khao village dining; Mai Khao Marine Turtle Foundation visitor area; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket about 20 km south for full grocery shopping; Phuket International Airport area for Makro and chain supermarkets.

Thalang Hospital — public (8 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (32 km); Mission Hospital Phuket in Phuket Town (35 km). No large private hospital on the north end; serious cases route to Bangkok Hospital Phuket by ambulance.

JW Marriott Phuket Resort beach bar, Anantara Mai Khao Villas pool bar and Sala Mai Khao restaurant, Renaissance Phuket Resort beachfront dining, Turtle Village casual restaurants, SALA Phuket Mai Khao beachfront restaurant.

Baan Mandala Villas is a luxurious complex of villas with its own infrastructure, located just 500 meters from the magnificent Bangtao Beach (Bang Tao) in the west of Phuket Island. Consists of eight magnificent luxury villas with tropical gardens and swimming pools, located in a closed area with 24-hour security. Offers luxury 2-4 bedroom villas on large plots with tropical gardens. The villas are built in a "U" shape around the pools. The interior spaces are designed in a simple yet elegant minimalist style with clean flowing lines and high teak ceilings to create bright and spacious living spaces with a sense of unparalleled spaciousness.

The infrastructure of the complex includes a reception, recreation area, gym, library, parking, round-the-clock security, etc.

Baan Mandala Villas is located in one of the most prestigious areas of Phuket with developed infrastructure. Therefore, the project is suitable for all those who prefer a measured rest surrounded by beautiful landscapes.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Nai Yang sits inside Sirinat National Park, just south of Mai Khao and a few minutes north of the airport. The bay is a long shallow arc with calm water in the dry season and proper Andaman swell in green season, which makes it one of the few west coast spots where local surfers actually gather. The village strip is small but real: a row of seafood restaurants facing the beach under the casuarina trees, a few dive shops, two yoga studios, a daily night market that sets up on the inland road and a small cluster of guesthouses. That mix gives Nai Yang a character that Mai Khao lacks. There is a village to walk to in the evening, a community of long-stay foreign residents who actually use it, and prices for both rentals and groceries are noticeably softer than down at Bang Tao. The resident expat profile leans toward families, retirees and remote workers who decided that proximity to the airport and a quieter beach mattered more than walking distance to Boat Avenue. Schools are 20 to 25 minutes south, hospitals are 30 minutes, and a car or scooter is essential. The Slate and Marriott resorts anchor the upper end of the dining scene, and the Carpe Diem and Coco Beach groups handle casual sunset crowds. Nai Yang rewards buyers who want a village feel without leaving the west coast.

Nai Yang village strip with seafood restaurants and beachfront cafes; Nai Yang night market (Thursdays and weekends) for cheap Thai food; The Slate resort dining hub; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket (about 18 km, 20 minutes south) for chain grocery and international restaurants; airport area Makro for bulk shopping.

Thalang Hospital — public (7 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (30 km); Mission Hospital Phuket (33 km). No large private hospital in the immediate north; expats typically register with Bangkok Hospital Phuket.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Nai Harn Beach Road and lagoon park; Rawai seafront (5 minutes east) for fresh seafood and weekly markets; Wyndham Grand Nai Harn and The Nai Harn hotel hubs for dining and gym access; Chalong Circle (10 km northeast) for Makro and visa offices.

Mission Hospital Phuket (14 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (18 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (17 km, public, major trauma centre).

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Hotel Cassia is located in the heart of Laguna Phuket Resort & Hotel Complex. It was built in 2015 and has become a favourite destination for tourists from all over the world. The hotel consists of two 6-storey buildings that are interconnected. The hotel is built in the Art Nouveau style, with very bright interiors of both the common areas and the apartments themselves. The number of rooms includes apartments with one and two bedrooms with or without a mezzanine. One bedroom apartments have a total area of ​​40-52 sq. m., mezzanine - 10-14 sq. m. Apartments with two bedrooms are more spacious - 62-86 sq. m. m. on the ground floor plus a mezzanine. All apartments have a kitchen fully equipped with household appliances and utensils and a dining table. In total, the hotel has 402 rooms, designed in the same style. The apartments offer magnificent views of the lake and the sea. Among the brands of Laguna, the Cassia apart-hotel stands out in that it is designed for a youth and active audience of holidaymakers. This is an affordable proposition, while the complex is surrounded by premium hotels, luxurious villas and world-class golf course.

The Cassia has a private beach equipped with sun loungers, a restaurant, a reception, two communal swimming pools with sun loungers and cabanas, showers and toilets, a bar and walking paths. There is a kids club for children, where you can just play and spend time. A free shuttle bus runs regularly from the complex to the beach and back. While resting at the Cassia Phuket hotel, you do not need to rent transport - by shuttle you can get to the beach, restaurants, shops, the main building. There is also a boat to the beach every half hour. This is especially convenient for families with small children. The restaurant offers in-villa or BBQ catering.

The Cassia complex is located right next to Bangtao Beach, which can be reached in 5 minutes on foot or by a free water bus that runs on the lake. This beach is where Phuket's most popular beach clubs are located, such as Xana Beach Club, Dream Beach Club and Catch Club. Next to Cassia is the Laguna Phuket golf club, where international class tournaments are held. Inexperienced golfers can use the services of a personal golf coach. Boat Avenue is a 2-minute drive from the Cassia, with a variety of shops, countless restaurants and bars, and Villa Market, a European supermarket. The modern Porto De Phuket shopping complex, with countless restaurants, Tors supermarket, boutiques and food court, is just a short drive away. Nearby is the Lemonade Kids Club with a children's room and a pool for children, a hot sauna for adults. The bustling party scene of Patong is a 30-minute drive from the complex. The road from the airport to the complex will take about 25 minutes.

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Chalong Circle with banks, Makro, Tesco Lotus and visa offices; Chalong Pier for island boats and seafood; Big Buddha access road; Villa Market in Chalong; Wat Chalong temple and surrounding local food strip; Friday Phuket Town night market 15 minutes north.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Coco Chalong is located on the south coast of Phuket and features 80 villas, each with a private pool, outdoor terraces and parking. 24-hour security, video surveillance, lush tropical garden, and a club area that includes a 15-meter pool, fully equipped fitness centre and restaurant.

It is worth noting the extremely convenient location of the Coco Chalong complex, it is not located in the centre of the tourist infrastructure of the south, but at the same time, such a location makes it accessible to tourist places and the entire infrastructure of the city. So, the Coco Chalong complex is located a few minutes drive from the Chalong pier, restaurants, massage parlours, large shopping centres where you can buy everything you need. An international school and kindergarten are just a short drive away. The famous fish market and the Rawai promenade are a 10-minute drive away. Phuket Zoo, Dolphinarium and Botanical Gardens are nearby. After driving 10 minutes you can find yourself on the best beaches of Nai Harn, Kata Noi and Kata, stunning with their views, sand and crystal clear sea. It will take no more time to get to such popular places in Thailand as Promthep Cape and Big Buddha. The drive to the largest tourist centre will take you 20 minutes, and the road to the airport is only 40 minutes.

The complex is suitable for both long-term stays and short vacations. It will be comfortable for both families with children and young couples.

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Chalong Circle with banks, Makro, Tesco Lotus and visa offices; Chalong Pier for island boats and seafood; Big Buddha access road; Villa Market in Chalong; Wat Chalong temple and surrounding local food strip; Friday Phuket Town night market 15 minutes north.

Mission Hospital Phuket (8 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (10 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (12 km, public, major trauma centre).

Kan Eang at Pier Restaurant (long established seafood institution on Chalong Bay), Greek Kitchen on the road to Big Buddha, Chalong Bay Rum Distillery and Mixing Lab (tours and cocktails), Latitude Sky Bar, On The Rock Restaurant at Marina Phuket Resort.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Since 1986, this beach has been part of the Sirinath National Park Marine Park and all motor sports are prohibited on it. There is a large selection of restaurants, bars and cafés along the beach. Nai Yang sits inside Sirinat National Park, just south of Mai Khao and a few minutes north of the airport. The bay is a long shallow arc with calm water in the dry season and proper Andaman swell in green season, which makes it one of the few west coast spots where local surfers actually gather. The village strip is small but real: a row of seafood restaurants facing the beach under the casuarina trees, a few dive shops, two yoga studios, a daily night market that sets up on the inland road and a small cluster of guesthouses. That mix gives Nai Yang a character that Mai Khao lacks. There is a village to walk to in the evening, a community of long-stay foreign residents who actually use it, and prices for both rentals and groceries are noticeably softer than down at Bang Tao. The resident expat profile leans toward families, retirees and remote workers who decided that proximity to the airport and a quieter beach mattered more than walking distance to Boat Avenue. Schools are 20 to 25 minutes south, hospitals are 30 minutes, and a car or scooter is essential. The Slate and Marriott resorts anchor the upper end of the dining scene, and the Carpe Diem and Coco Beach groups handle casual sunset crowds. Nai Yang rewards buyers who want a village feel without leaving the west coast.

Nai Yang village strip with seafood restaurants and beachfront cafes; Nai Yang night market (Thursdays and weekends) for cheap Thai food; The Slate resort dining hub; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket (about 18 km, 20 minutes south) for chain grocery and international restaurants; airport area Makro for bulk shopping.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.
