Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Kamala Beach Road with cafes and dive shops; Cafe del Mar Phuket area (beachfront events and dining); Plaza del Mar boutique mall; Kamala Fresh Market on the main road; Cherngtalay corridor reachable in 10 minutes north.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Mai Khao is the longest beach on Phuket, an 11 kilometre stretch on the very north end of the island, mostly protected as part of Sirinat National Park. Because of that protection, the coastline is almost free of the usual shophouse strip. Development here means a thin line of large resorts, JW Marriott, Anantara, Renaissance, SALA, Marriott Vacation Club, set behind a wide casuarina belt, with very little outside them. Foreign residents in Mai Khao are typically owners inside one of the branded residences attached to those resorts, or buyers in the small condo and villa clusters that sit just inland of the highway. The community is small, older and quiet, with a strong share of European and Asian second-home owners who use the property a few months a year. The main practical advantage of living here is the airport, which is six to ten minutes by car, so travel-heavy buyers and pilots actually consider it the best base on the island. The trade-off is the rest of the infrastructure. There is no real town strip, no walking grocery, and a trip to the international schools or major hospital is a 25 minute drive south. The beach itself is fantastic: empty most of the year, with sea turtles still nesting in season, and a noticeable absence of jet skis.

Turtle Village shopping plaza next to JW Marriott (cafes, mini-mart, small boutiques); Anantara Mai Khao village dining; Mai Khao Marine Turtle Foundation visitor area; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket about 20 km south for full grocery shopping; Phuket International Airport area for Makro and chain supermarkets.

Thalang Hospital — public (8 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (32 km); Mission Hospital Phuket in Phuket Town (35 km). No large private hospital on the north end; serious cases route to Bangkok Hospital Phuket by ambulance.

JW Marriott Phuket Resort beach bar, Anantara Mai Khao Villas pool bar and Sala Mai Khao restaurant, Renaissance Phuket Resort beachfront dining, Turtle Village casual restaurants, SALA Phuket Mai Khao beachfront restaurant.

Nai Yang sits inside Sirinat National Park, just south of Mai Khao and a few minutes north of the airport. The bay is a long shallow arc with calm water in the dry season and proper Andaman swell in green season, which makes it one of the few west coast spots where local surfers actually gather. The village strip is small but real: a row of seafood restaurants facing the beach under the casuarina trees, a few dive shops, two yoga studios, a daily night market that sets up on the inland road and a small cluster of guesthouses. That mix gives Nai Yang a character that Mai Khao lacks. There is a village to walk to in the evening, a community of long-stay foreign residents who actually use it, and prices for both rentals and groceries are noticeably softer than down at Bang Tao. The resident expat profile leans toward families, retirees and remote workers who decided that proximity to the airport and a quieter beach mattered more than walking distance to Boat Avenue. Schools are 20 to 25 minutes south, hospitals are 30 minutes, and a car or scooter is essential. The Slate and Marriott resorts anchor the upper end of the dining scene, and the Carpe Diem and Coco Beach groups handle casual sunset crowds. Nai Yang rewards buyers who want a village feel without leaving the west coast.

Nai Yang village strip with seafood restaurants and beachfront cafes; Nai Yang night market (Thursdays and weekends) for cheap Thai food; The Slate resort dining hub; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket (about 18 km, 20 minutes south) for chain grocery and international restaurants; airport area Makro for bulk shopping.

Thalang Hospital — public (7 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (30 km); Mission Hospital Phuket (33 km). No large private hospital in the immediate north; expats typically register with Bangkok Hospital Phuket.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Dynasty Group's new ISOLA project won the 2020 Dot Property Thailand Awards for Best New Launch Villa Development, Phuket, thanks in part to its unique design that helps it stand out from other projects on the market. The developer's mission is to exceed what other developers do and maintain a constant difference. The developer does this so that in the event of deteriorating market conditions, its projects are distinguished, and the owners and investors always have security when renting and resale. ISOLA is distinguished by its distinctive modern architecture and its hotel style in a residential area. Many aspects of ISOLA Phuket have been inspired by the worldwide popular ultra-luxury villa market. The Dynasty Group's goal was to launch a villa with the same level of service and attention to detail, but at an affordable price. The complex consists of 12 exquisite two-storey villas with 2 and 3 bedrooms with infinity pools. The villas offer standard floor plans and luxurious interiors. The project was designed for owners, and everything from infinity pools and huge floor-to-ceiling glass windows to individual outdoor lounges and cantilevered balconies was created for these buyers.

The project offers residents a personal concierge, butler and cleaning services that reflects the level of service of a 5-star hotel. The team will be able to organize your agenda, the butler will do your laundry, recommend restaurants, collect your purchases, or whatever you ask the hotel concierge. This is in addition to the chef who can prepare meals in the privacy of your own villa. Residents' speedboat will also be offered to owners, allowing them to explore the neighbouring islands of Phuket. There will be two gyms and a reception on the territory.

The project is located close to Layan Beach, part of the island where 5-star resorts are located, and just 5 minutes drive from Bangtao Beach. This beach is where Phuket's most popular beach clubs are located, such as Xana Beach Club, Dream Beach Club and Catch Club. Next to Angsana Villas Resort is the Laguna Phuket Golf Club, which hosts international class tournaments. Inexperienced golfers can use the services of a personal golf coach. A 10-minute drive from Angsana Villas is the Boat Avenue shopping complex with a variety of shops, restaurants and bars, and a European supermarket Villa Market. The modern Porto De Phuket shopping complex, with countless restaurants, Tors supermarket, boutiques and food court, is just a short drive away. Nearby is the Lemonade Kids Club with a children's room and a pool for children, a hot sauna for adults. The bustling party scene of Patong is a 30-minute drive from the complex. The road from the airport to the complex will take about 25 minutes.

For buyers who value luxury, conservative and discreet, for those who want to live in a quiet residential complex that provides maximum privacy and security at all times, while maintaining the highest level of design detail in the world.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Karon Beach Road promenade with restaurants and bars; Karon Plaza shopping strip; Karon Temple Market (Tuesdays and Fridays) for Thai street food and clothing; Big C Karon and Karon Bazaar for groceries; Kata Centre and Beach Road 5 minutes south for additional restaurants and shopping; The Movenpick Karon and Hilton Arcadia hotel hubs.

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Karon Beach Road promenade with restaurants and bars; Karon Plaza shopping strip; Karon Temple Market (Tuesdays and Fridays) for Thai street food and clothing; Big C Karon and Karon Bazaar for groceries; Kata Centre and Beach Road 5 minutes south for additional restaurants and shopping; The Movenpick Karon and Hilton Arcadia hotel hubs.

Kata sits on the southwest coast, two bays south of Patong and one north of Nai Harn. The area is built around two beaches, Kata Yai and the smaller Kata Noi, both with cleaner sand and calmer water than Patong, plus a reliable surf break from May to October that keeps a small but committed long-stay surf community on the island year round. The foreign population here splits into three groups: surf and dive instructors who came on a season and stayed, retirees who chose Kata over Rawai for direct beach access, and remote workers who rent condos in Kata Hills for the views. Day to day life is walkable along Kata Beach Road and Patak Road, with bakeries, Thai kitchens, two small supermarkets and a steady rotation of cafes opening and closing each season. Nightlife is low key compared to Patong: a handful of bars, the Ska Bar sundowner spot under the banyan tree, and the weekend Kata Night Market for street food. Schools require a car, with Kajonkiet the closest international option and the Phuket Town cluster reachable in 25 to 30 minutes. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the Chalong side of the hill. The trade-offs are real high season traffic on the Patak hill road and limited supermarket options on site, but Kata works well for buyers who want a proper beach lifestyle without Patong density.

Kata Beach Road with cafes, dive shops and surf rentals; Kata Night Market (weekends) on Patak Road; Karon Plaza shopping strip (3 km north); Big C and Tesco Lotus in Chalong (10 km east) for full grocery runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (14 km, JCI-accredited); Karon Sub-District Health Promotion Hospital (2 km, public clinic).

Kata Rocks Clubhouse and Infinity Bar, Mom Tri Kitchen at Boathouse, Ska Bar (under the banyan tree, southern end of Kata Beach), Re Ka Ta Beach Club at Katathani, Oasis Restaurant and Bar.

We present to you an exquisite hilltop retreat, where the expanse of Chalong Bay opens up before you like a picture. When you turn around, your gaze rests on the picturesque mountains, shrouded in evergreen forest. This is Chalong Temple, a place where modern design and wild nature create a harmonious unity. The location of the villa is ideal: here, close to attractions, supermarkets and restaurants, you will find your corner of silence just 38 kilometers from the airport.

Immerse yourself in a world of elegant luxury with our 814 square meter villas with seductive sea and sunset views. Three separate pavilions of the villa open up to you the shimmering expanse of the sea, and the 3-meter ceilings give it a special exquisite charm, creating an airy and relaxing atmosphere. At Chalong Temple you will plunge into a world of tranquility and privacy.

Looking for a quiet luxury getaway, but still want to enjoy all the variety that Phuket has to offer? Chalong Temple is made just for you.

Seclusion in this place does not mean remoteness from life: the noisy streets of hotels and villages remain outside, but all the main infrastructure of the island - international schools, hospitals, shopping centers - are only 15 minutes away.

The total area of the building is 731 sq. m., plot area 814 sq. m.

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Chalong Circle with banks, Makro, Tesco Lotus and visa offices; Chalong Pier for island boats and seafood; Big Buddha access road; Villa Market in Chalong; Wat Chalong temple and surrounding local food strip; Friday Phuket Town night market 15 minutes north.

Mission Hospital Phuket (8 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (10 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (12 km, public, major trauma centre).

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Karon Beach Road promenade with restaurants and bars; Karon Plaza shopping strip; Karon Temple Market (Tuesdays and Fridays) for Thai street food and clothing; Big C Karon and Karon Bazaar for groceries; Kata Centre and Beach Road 5 minutes south for additional restaurants and shopping; The Movenpick Karon and Hilton Arcadia hotel hubs.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

Комплекс Кокянг расположен на юге острова Пхукет, в центре популярного района Най-Харна, всего лишь в 5 минутах езды от пляжа ив 150 метрах от ресторанов и кафе. Виллы с 2 и 3 спальнями спроектированы буквой L из панорамных окон комнат открывается вид на бассейн. Все виллы прекрасно декорированы и комфортны для проживания. Вилла с 3 спальнями состоит из двух здании. В первом размещена просторная гостиная, которая объединена с кухней и две спальни, с приватными ванными комнатами. Во втором - спальня с отдельной ванной комнатой. При выходе из виллы Вы окажетесь на террасе рядом с личным бассейном. Возле каждой виллы есть парковочное место под крышей.

Магазины, рестораны и массаж, находятся в шаговой доступности.

Один из лучших пляжей - Найхарн находится в 3 километрах от проекта. Пляж пользуется популярностью у семей с детьми и экспатов, по этому здесь вы не встретите большое скопление туристов. В двух шагах от пляжа есть пресноводное озеро и смотровая площадка с ветряными мельницами. Пляж Най Харн пользуется популярностью у семей с детьми, а также у зимовщиков и долгожителей острова. Отпуск здесь проводить комфортно, т.к. рядом множество ресторанов как европейской. так и национальной тайской кухни. Здесь же есть офисы с арендой транспорта и экскурсионными услугами. Для длительного проживания на Найхарне комфортно жить семьям с детьми - рядом расположены международные и тайские детские сады, интернациональные и русская школы. Путь от Найхарна до популярного детского игрового комплекс «Раваи парк» займет 5 минут на авто или байке.

Также Найхарн часто выбирают для йога-туров или спортивных кемпингов. На Найхарне и в соседнем с ним районе Раваи сосредоточены спортивные залы, специализированные ринги для занятий тайским боксом и площадки для воркаута. В 5 минутах езды находится гипер маркет Макро, супермаркет с европейскими продуктами Villa Market, рыбный рынок. Так же в этом районе сконцентрировано максимальное количество школ и детских садов.

Комплекс идеально подходит абсолютно всем категориям туристов. Отличное место для отдыха с детьми и для пар и компаний любого возраста. Виллы в проекте доступны, как для коротких каникул, так и для долгосрочной аренды.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Lake Residences is the third phase of the large-scale Gardens of Eden development in the Layan–Bang Tao area of Phuket. Created by Amal Development with architecture and landscape design by Tierra Design and Wonder by White Jacket, the project is built around a strong nature-focused and wellness-driven philosophy. Lake Residences is set along a scenic lake within the masterplan and offers a calm, park-like environment with extensive greenery, water features, and low building density. This phase consists of nine residential buildings with a total of 698 units, all positioned around the lake with a 150-metre pool and approximately 5,000 square metres of water surface, including areas with colorful fish. The development features underground parking with elevator access, keeping the internal spaces peaceful and free from traffic.

Gardens of Eden places a strong emphasis on lifestyle and wellbeing. Around 70% of the entire land area is dedicated to open green spaces, landscaped gardens, and recreational zones. Residents will have access to a wide range of facilities, including a large wellness center of about 5,000 square metres, multiple jogging and walking trails totaling 3.5 kilometres, kids’ play areas and clubs, two clubhouses, an open-air cinema, a pet park, several on-site restaurants, a business center, and a small supermarket. The broader development also incorporates an 80-room hotel, adding to the overall convenience and service level. Materials, design elements, and landscaping throughout the project follow a biophilic, eco-minded approach with a focus on natural materials and an abundance of greenery.

Lake Residences offers units on a long-term leasehold basis with a 90-year structure, while freehold ownership is available by request for an additional cost. Furniture packages are provided separately. Completion for this phase is targeted for the third quarter of 2028. Since it is an off-plan development, buyers should consider typical construction and delivery risks, along with the leasehold structure and long investment horizon. Despite this, the project stands out for its large scale, wellness concept, extensive facilities, and rare amount of natural open space, making it appealing for both long-term living and high-end resort-style use.

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Chalong Circle with banks, Makro, Tesco Lotus and visa offices; Chalong Pier for island boats and seafood; Big Buddha access road; Villa Market in Chalong; Wat Chalong temple and surrounding local food strip; Friday Phuket Town night market 15 minutes north.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Kamala Beach Road with cafes and dive shops; Cafe del Mar Phuket area (beachfront events and dining); Plaza del Mar boutique mall; Kamala Fresh Market on the main road; Cherngtalay corridor reachable in 10 minutes north.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (16 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (15 km, public, major trauma centre).

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Boat Avenue (about 4 km south in Cherngtalay); Porto de Phuket (4 km south); Laguna Phuket complex (3 km, golf, lagoons, spas); Layan village small strip with local restaurants and marts.

Bangkok Hospital Phuket (23 km); Thalang Hospital — public (8 km); Bangkok Hospital Siriroj (25 km).

Mai Khao is the longest beach on Phuket, an 11 kilometre stretch on the very north end of the island, mostly protected as part of Sirinat National Park. Because of that protection, the coastline is almost free of the usual shophouse strip. Development here means a thin line of large resorts, JW Marriott, Anantara, Renaissance, SALA, Marriott Vacation Club, set behind a wide casuarina belt, with very little outside them. Foreign residents in Mai Khao are typically owners inside one of the branded residences attached to those resorts, or buyers in the small condo and villa clusters that sit just inland of the highway. The community is small, older and quiet, with a strong share of European and Asian second-home owners who use the property a few months a year. The main practical advantage of living here is the airport, which is six to ten minutes by car, so travel-heavy buyers and pilots actually consider it the best base on the island. The trade-off is the rest of the infrastructure. There is no real town strip, no walking grocery, and a trip to the international schools or major hospital is a 25 minute drive south. The beach itself is fantastic: empty most of the year, with sea turtles still nesting in season, and a noticeable absence of jet skis.

Turtle Village shopping plaza next to JW Marriott (cafes, mini-mart, small boutiques); Anantara Mai Khao village dining; Mai Khao Marine Turtle Foundation visitor area; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket about 20 km south for full grocery shopping; Phuket International Airport area for Makro and chain supermarkets.

Thalang Hospital — public (8 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (32 km); Mission Hospital Phuket in Phuket Town (35 km). No large private hospital on the north end; serious cases route to Bangkok Hospital Phuket by ambulance.

JW Marriott Phuket Resort beach bar, Anantara Mai Khao Villas pool bar and Sala Mai Khao restaurant, Renaissance Phuket Resort beachfront dining, Turtle Village casual restaurants, SALA Phuket Mai Khao beachfront restaurant.

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Mai Khao is the longest beach on Phuket, an 11 kilometre stretch on the very north end of the island, mostly protected as part of Sirinat National Park. Because of that protection, the coastline is almost free of the usual shophouse strip. Development here means a thin line of large resorts, JW Marriott, Anantara, Renaissance, SALA, Marriott Vacation Club, set behind a wide casuarina belt, with very little outside them. Foreign residents in Mai Khao are typically owners inside one of the branded residences attached to those resorts, or buyers in the small condo and villa clusters that sit just inland of the highway. The community is small, older and quiet, with a strong share of European and Asian second-home owners who use the property a few months a year. The main practical advantage of living here is the airport, which is six to ten minutes by car, so travel-heavy buyers and pilots actually consider it the best base on the island. The trade-off is the rest of the infrastructure. There is no real town strip, no walking grocery, and a trip to the international schools or major hospital is a 25 minute drive south. The beach itself is fantastic: empty most of the year, with sea turtles still nesting in season, and a noticeable absence of jet skis.

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Nai Thon is one of the last properly quiet beaches on the Phuket west coast. The bay sits inside the Sirinat National Park buffer, which has kept large-scale development out and left a narrow village strip facing a clean, swimmable beach. Most foreign residents here are not first-time arrivals: they tend to be retirees, returning travellers and families looking specifically for low density living. The trade-off is straightforward. You get a calm beach, jungle hills behind, almost no traffic, and a 10 to 15 minute drive to Phuket International Airport. In exchange you accept that the international schools, Boat Avenue and the large hospitals are 20 to 30 minutes south, which makes a car or scooter essentially mandatory. Day to day, life revolves around the village strip: a row of beachfront restaurants, a couple of small mini-marts, dive shops and yoga studios. Nai Yang, five minutes south, adds a Thai night market and the Marriott and Slate resort hubs for weekend dining. Healthcare is the main thing to think about: there is no large private hospital in the immediate north, so most expats register with Bangkok Hospital Phuket and rely on its ambulance network. For buyers, Nai Thon attracts those who specifically reject the Bang Tao density, and the rental yield profile is different, with strong high-season occupancy and a softer green season.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

The Oasis development has been designed to foster a sense of community while maintaining a serene and secure environment. The village is safeguarded by 24/7 security, ensuring peace of mind for its residents. The landscape design is harmonized throughout the community, featuring roof gardens and terraces that blend seamlessly with the natural surroundings.

A key philosophy of the Oasis project is its commitment to providing homes that are completely ready for occupancy. The concept of “Absolute Homespace” ensures that each villa is delivered fully furnished and equipped, from furniture arrangements to kitchen setups. This attention to detail eliminates the need for renovations or additional preparations, offering residents a seamless transition into their new home.

The project’s location also places residents in proximity to a wealth of attractions. Dining and entertainment options abound, with destinations such as Boat Avenue and the Bang Tao Night Market offering vibrant experiences. Beach clubs like Catch and Maya provide lively nightlife, while the Laguna Golf Club caters to golf enthusiasts. For those seeking leisure and shopping, options such as the Green Elephant Sanctuary Park, Central Phuket Festival Mall, and Tesco Lotus are just a short drive away.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (16 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (15 km, public, major trauma centre).

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Karon Beach Road promenade with restaurants and bars; Karon Plaza shopping strip; Karon Temple Market (Tuesdays and Fridays) for Thai street food and clothing; Big C Karon and Karon Bazaar for groceries; Kata Centre and Beach Road 5 minutes south for additional restaurants and shopping; The Movenpick Karon and Hilton Arcadia hotel hubs.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Motorboats leave from Rawai Promenade to the neighbouring islands.

The nearest bathing beach, Nai Harn, is a 10-minute drive from the complex. The beach is popular with families with children and expats, so you will not find a large crowd of tourists here. It is comfortable to spend your holiday here, because Nearby there are many restaurants of both European and national Thai cuisine. There are also offices with transport rental and excursion services.

Also, within a radius of 5-10 kilometres there are Russian and Thai kindergartens, international, international and Russian schools.

In the Rawai district and in the neighbouring Naiharn district, there are gyms, specialized rings for Thai boxing and workout grounds. In 7-10 minutes drive there is a hyper market Makro, a supermarket with European products Villa Market, a fish market. Super grocery stores: Tesco Lotus, Macro, Villa Market, seafood market in Rawai, numerous convenience stores (7-Eleven Super Cheap, Family Mart).

Different configurations of villas make it comfortable for different categories of tourists. Most often, villas are chosen here for permanent residence or for long-term vacations.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.
