Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Day to day life is walkable along Kata Beach Road and Patak Road, with bakeries, Thai kitchens, two small supermarkets and a steady rotation of cafes opening and closing each season. The trade-offs are real high season traffic on the Patak hill road and limited supermarket options on site, but Kata works well for buyers who want a proper beach lifestyle without Patong density.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Mission Hospital Phuket (14 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (18 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (17 km, public, major trauma centre).

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Nai Thon is one of the last properly quiet beaches on the Phuket west coast. The bay sits inside the Sirinat National Park buffer, which has kept large-scale development out and left a narrow village strip facing a clean, swimmable beach. Most foreign residents here are not first-time arrivals: they tend to be retirees, returning travellers and families looking specifically for low density living. The trade-off is straightforward. You get a calm beach, jungle hills behind, almost no traffic, and a 10 to 15 minute drive to Phuket International Airport. In exchange you accept that the international schools, Boat Avenue and the large hospitals are 20 to 30 minutes south, which makes a car or scooter essentially mandatory. Day to day, life revolves around the village strip: a row of beachfront restaurants, a couple of small mini-marts, dive shops and yoga studios. Nai Yang, five minutes south, adds a Thai night market and the Marriott and Slate resort hubs for weekend dining. Healthcare is the main thing to think about: there is no large private hospital in the immediate north, so most expats register with Bangkok Hospital Phuket and rely on its ambulance network. For buyers, Nai Thon attracts those who specifically reject the Bang Tao density, and the rental yield profile is different, with strong high-season occupancy and a softer green season.

Nai Thon village strip (beachfront cafes, mini-marts, dive shops); Nai Yang village 5 km south for night market and casual dining; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket (about 15 km, 20 minutes south); Phuket International Airport area for chain supermarkets.

Thalang Hospital — public (10 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (30 km); Mission Hospital Phuket in Phuket Town (32 km). Note: no large private hospital on site; ambulance transfer to Bangkok Hospital Phuket is the standard route.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Saiyuan Med Village, a complex located in the south of Phuket, a 10-minute drive from one of the best beaches in Phuket, Naiharn Beach. The construction of the complex was completed in 2010. In a closed area there are several asphalted streets where 63 Mediterranean style villas with 2, 3, 4 and 5 bedrooms, ranging from 120 m2 to 240 m2, are comfortably located. All houses on the outside are made in the same architectural style, but at the same time they have different layouts and designs. The project has villas with a private pool, each house has its own parking.

The complex is under round-the-clock security, on the territory there is an office of the management company, a communal pool and a playground.

The complex is located in an area with a developed tourist infrastructure, close to restaurants, massage parlours, and 24-hour mini-markets. One of the best beaches - Naiharn is a 10-minute drive from the projects. The beach is popular with families with children and expats, so you will not find a large crowd of tourists here. A stone's throw from the beach, there is a freshwater lake and an observation deck with windmills. Nai Harn Beach is popular with families with children, as well as with winterers and long-livers of the island. It is comfortable to spend your vacation here, because Nearby there are many restaurants like European, and national Thai cuisine. There are also offices with transport rental and excursion services. For a long stay on Naiharn, it is comfortable to live for families with children - there are international and Thai kindergartens, international and Russian schools nearby. The way from Naiharn to the popular children's play complex "Rawai Park" will take 5 minutes by car or bike.

Naiharn is also often chosen for yoga tours or sports campings. At Naiharn and in the neighbouring Rawai district, there are gyms, specialized rings for Thai boxing and workout grounds. In 7-10 minutes drive there is a hyper market Makro, a supermarket with European products Villa Market, a fish market.

The complex is ideal for absolutely everyone. Different sizes of villas and pricing policies will allow each category of tourists to spend their holidays in comfort. Especially popular with families with children and expats. Most often it is chosen for long-term residence. The location of the villas ensures privacy and comfort.

Nai Thon is one of the last properly quiet beaches on the Phuket west coast. The bay sits inside the Sirinat National Park buffer, which has kept large-scale development out and left a narrow village strip facing a clean, swimmable beach. Most foreign residents here are not first-time arrivals: they tend to be retirees, returning travellers and families looking specifically for low density living. The trade-off is straightforward. You get a calm beach, jungle hills behind, almost no traffic, and a 10 to 15 minute drive to Phuket International Airport. In exchange you accept that the international schools, Boat Avenue and the large hospitals are 20 to 30 minutes south, which makes a car or scooter essentially mandatory. Day to day, life revolves around the village strip: a row of beachfront restaurants, a couple of small mini-marts, dive shops and yoga studios. Nai Yang, five minutes south, adds a Thai night market and the Marriott and Slate resort hubs for weekend dining. Healthcare is the main thing to think about: there is no large private hospital in the immediate north, so most expats register with Bangkok Hospital Phuket and rely on its ambulance network. For buyers, Nai Thon attracts those who specifically reject the Bang Tao density, and the rental yield profile is different, with strong high-season occupancy and a softer green season.

Nai Thon village strip (beachfront cafes, mini-marts, dive shops); Nai Yang village 5 km south for night market and casual dining; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket (about 15 km, 20 minutes south); Phuket International Airport area for chain supermarkets.

Thalang Hospital — public (10 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (30 km); Mission Hospital Phuket in Phuket Town (32 km). Note: no large private hospital on site; ambulance transfer to Bangkok Hospital Phuket is the standard route.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Apartment types include duplex, studio and 1-2 bedrooms. Each apartment has a large terrace with sea or mountain views. Also, private villas will be built on the territory of the complex. The new project will be built on the first line of Naithon Beach. The complex will consist of 5- and 8-storey buildings with apartments ranging from 27 to 70 sq.m. Apartment types include duplex, studio and 1-2 bedrooms. Each apartment has a large terrace with sea or mountain views. Also, private villas will be built on the territory of the complex. In the common area of ​​the complex, guests and owners have a large landscaped communal pool with jacuzzi, gym, reception and underground and ground parking. There are sun loungers with umbrellas by the pool, as well as a Thai gazebo for relaxation. The complex is fully guarded 24 hours a day. Just imagine how convenient it is, because you no longer have to waste precious time on the road to the sea. The desire to bathe will be immediately realised. Nai Thon is one of the last properly quiet beaches on the Phuket west coast. The bay sits inside the Sirinat National Park buffer, which has kept large-scale development out and left a narrow village strip facing a clean, swimmable beach. Most foreign residents here are not first-time arrivals: they tend to be retirees, returning travellers and families looking specifically for low density living. The trade-off is straightforward. You get a calm beach, jungle hills behind, almost no traffic, and a 10 to 15 minute drive to Phuket International Airport. In exchange you accept that the international schools, Boat Avenue and the large hospitals are 20 to 30 minutes south, which makes a car or scooter essentially mandatory. Day to day, life revolves around the village strip: a row of beachfront restaurants, a couple of small mini-marts, dive shops and yoga studios. Nai Yang, five minutes south, adds a Thai night market and the Marriott and Slate resort hubs for weekend dining. Healthcare is the main thing to think about: there is no large private hospital in the immediate north, so most expats register with Bangkok Hospital Phuket and rely on its ambulance network. For buyers, Nai Thon attracts those who specifically reject the Bang Tao density, and the rental yield profile is different, with strong high-season occupancy and a softer green season.

Nai Thon village strip (beachfront cafes, mini-marts, dive shops); Nai Yang village 5 km south for night market and casual dining; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket (about 15 km, 20 minutes south); Phuket International Airport area for chain supermarkets.

Thalang Hospital — public (10 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (30 km); Mission Hospital Phuket in Phuket Town (32 km). Note: no large private hospital on site; ambulance transfer to Bangkok Hospital Phuket is the standard route.

Andaman Restaurant Nai Thon (beachfront), Coco Beach Restaurant Nai Yang, The Slate beach restaurants at Nai Yang, Phuket Marriott Resort and Spa Nai Yang beachfront bar, Trisara private beach restaurant (between Nai Thon and Layan).

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Karon Beach Road promenade with restaurants and bars; Karon Plaza shopping strip; Karon Temple Market (Tuesdays and Fridays) for Thai street food and clothing; Big C Karon and Karon Bazaar for groceries; Kata Centre and Beach Road 5 minutes south for additional restaurants and shopping; The Movenpick Karon and Hilton Arcadia hotel hubs.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (16 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (15 km, public, major trauma centre).

SO Origin Kata Phuket is a new luxury condominium just 800 meters from Kata Beach and 350 meters from Kata Night Plaza. Developed by Origin Property, this low-rise project combines modern design with a tropical lifestyle, offering both comfort and convenience in one of Phuket’s most desirable beachside neighborhoods.

The project covers over 23,000 square meters of green space and includes 686 residences across four 8-storey buildings. Unit types range from compact studios of 26 square meters, practical one-bedroom layouts from 30 to 40 square meters, and spacious two-bedroom apartments from 65 to 75 square meters. All units are designed with premium finishes, functional layouts, and contemporary interiors to maximize space and comfort.

Residents enjoy a wide selection of facilities across 11 lifestyle zones, including swimming pools, landscaped gardens, fitness center, steam rooms, co-working spaces, a sunset terrace, and dedicated relaxation areas. The development also provides 24-hour security, CCTV, and a welcoming clubhouse lobby.

The location offers the perfect balance of tranquility and connectivity. Kata Beach is only a short walk away, with Karon and Patong beaches also nearby. Shopping options such as Kata Night Plaza, local shops, and Central Floresta in Phuket Town are within easy reach. Essential services like hospitals and international schools are also close, making it convenient for both families and long-term residents.

SO Origin Kata Phuket presents an ideal choice for those seeking a modern condominium by the sea, with resort-style amenities, a prime location, and strong investment potential.

Kata sits on the southwest coast, two bays south of Patong and one north of Nai Harn. The area is built around two beaches, Kata Yai and the smaller Kata Noi, both with cleaner sand and calmer water than Patong, plus a reliable surf break from May to October that keeps a small but committed long-stay surf community on the island year round. The foreign population here splits into three groups: surf and dive instructors who came on a season and stayed, retirees who chose Kata over Rawai for direct beach access, and remote workers who rent condos in Kata Hills for the views. Day to day life is walkable along Kata Beach Road and Patak Road, with bakeries, Thai kitchens, two small supermarkets and a steady rotation of cafes opening and closing each season. Nightlife is low key compared to Patong: a handful of bars, the Ska Bar sundowner spot under the banyan tree, and the weekend Kata Night Market for street food. Schools require a car, with Kajonkiet the closest international option and the Phuket Town cluster reachable in 25 to 30 minutes. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the Chalong side of the hill. The trade-offs are real high season traffic on the Patak hill road and limited supermarket options on site, but Kata works well for buyers who want a proper beach lifestyle without Patong density.

Kata Beach Road with cafes, dive shops and surf rentals; Kata Night Market (weekends) on Patak Road; Karon Plaza shopping strip (3 km north); Big C and Tesco Lotus in Chalong (10 km east) for full grocery runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (14 km, JCI-accredited); Karon Sub-District Health Promotion Hospital (2 km, public clinic).

Kata Rocks Clubhouse and Infinity Bar, Mom Tri Kitchen at Boathouse, Ska Bar (under the banyan tree, southern end of Kata Beach), Re Ka Ta Beach Club at Katathani, Oasis Restaurant and Bar.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Kamala Beach Road with cafes and dive shops; Cafe del Mar Phuket area (beachfront events and dining); Plaza del Mar boutique mall; Kamala Fresh Market on the main road; Cherngtalay corridor reachable in 10 minutes north.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Karon is the middle option on the southwest coast, sitting between the noise of Patong to the north and the surf village calm of Kata to the south. The beach itself is the second longest on Phuket, around three kilometres of white sand with a real shore break in the green season, which is why local surfers, kite-surfers and Russian and Scandinavian families have gravitated here for the past two decades. Karon never went fully boutique like Surin or fully party like Patong; instead it built a steady middle market of small hotels, condo blocks and family-run restaurants along the inland road. The foreign resident scene reflects that. Long-term Russians and Ukrainians make up a large share, alongside Scandinavians, British retirees and a smaller French and German contingent, plus a steady flow of repeat seasonal visitors who eventually bought condos in the Karon Hills area. Daily life is straightforward. You can walk to the beach from most central blocks, the Tuesday and Friday temple market handles cheap Thai food and clothing, Big C Karon covers groceries, and a five minute drive to Kata Centre opens up better restaurants and the surf scene. International schools are a 15 to 20 minute drive over to Chalong or Phuket Town. Karon suits buyers who want a real swimming beach within walking distance, mid-range pricing and an established foreign community.

Karon Beach Road promenade with restaurants and bars; Karon Plaza shopping strip; Karon Temple Market (Tuesdays and Fridays) for Thai street food and clothing; Big C Karon and Karon Bazaar for groceries; Kata Centre and Beach Road 5 minutes south for additional restaurants and shopping; The Movenpick Karon and Hilton Arcadia hotel hubs.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

This beautiful 3-bedroom villa is located in Surin Beach, Phuket and is available for sale. Situated on a 1360 square meter plot, the villa offers a spacious and lush environment. The villa itself spans 380 square meters and features 3 bedrooms and 4 bathrooms.

Completed in January 2004, this Thai/Bali style villa is a top-quality property. Its prime location allows for a 7-minute walk or a 3-minute drive to the pristine beaches of Surin and Bangtao. Surin Beach is known for its clear waters, excellent snorkeling, and brilliant white sand.

The villa boasts a comfortable and cozy living space, complemented by an open and beautifully landscaped garden. A swimming pool adds to the relaxation and enjoyment of the property. Additionally, there are three excellent local restaurants, as well as massage and gym facilities, just minutes away.

Convenience is a key feature, as the villa provides easy access to the airport, international schools, Laguna, Patong, and Phuket town. All of these destinations are within a 25-minute drive.

Villa ensures a smooth and secure ownership transfer. Furthermore, being an independent villa, there are no common area maintenance fees (CAM fees) or water fees associated with the property.

This tropical 3-bedroom villa in Surin Beach, Phuket offers a perfect blend of elegance, comfort, and convenience. It presents a wonderful opportunity for those seeking a beautiful and well-located residence in Phuket.

name: Chalong — Tamarind Villa
description:
Tamarind Villa is a project of 32 villas in Chalong, Phuket, completed in 2011. 2 properties are available for rent. Distance to the sea: 9 km.

Tamarind Villa Phuket is a villa complex located in the most picturesque, southern part of Phuket Island, between Chalong and Rawai bays in an exceptionally quiet and cozy place that has preserved its pristine beauty. There are only two two-bedroom villas and two four-bedroom villas in the complex. The remaining 28 villas in the project are three bedroom villas. Each of the villas is a cozy home with a modern, stylish design. The spacious living room is combined with a modern fully equipped kitchen, with a dining table, two

Tamarind Villa Phuket is a villa complex located in the most picturesque, southern part of Phuket Island, between Chalong and Rawai bays in an exceptionally quiet and cozy place that has preserved its pristine beauty. There are only two two-bedroom villas and two four-bedroom villas in the complex. The remaining 28 villas in the project are three bedroom villas. Each of the villas is a cozy home with a modern, stylish design. The spacious living room is combined with a modern fully equipped kitchen, with a dining table, two bedrooms with king size beds, the third guest bedroom has two single beds. Each of the bedrooms has private bathrooms with walk-in showers, and the master also has a summer outdoor rain shower. Each villa has a rooftop outdoor terrace equipped with a ceiling fan with a large dining table, private pool, small garden and sun lounger area.

All 32 villas in the project are immersed in the greenery of tropical trees, the houses are designed in the same architectural style, which creates an indescribable atmosphere of coziness and comfort, as soon as you enter the territory of this complex, which has its own round-the-clock security, tennis court, management service and green well-groomed territory for hiking and cycling trips and a restaurant where you can order directly to the villa.

The complex is well located in relation to the 4 beaches of the island - Nai Harn, Rawai, Kata, Kata Noi. Two minutes drive from the major supermarkets Villa Market and Makro, in close proximity to international schools and kindergartens and attractions such as Phuket Orchid Farm, Phuket Shooting Range, Phuket Sports and Tennis Club.

One of the best beaches - Nai Harn is located 9 kilometers from the project. The beach is popular with families with children and expats, so you will not find a large crowd of tourists here. A stone's throw from the beach, there is a freshwater lake and an observation deck with windmills. Nai Harn Beach is popular with families with children, as well as those who prefer a long-stay on the island. It is comfortable to spend your vacation here, because Nearby there are many restaurants like European. and national Thai cuisine. There are also offices with transport rental and excursion services. For a long stay on Nai Harn, it is comfortable to live for families with children - there are international and Thai kindergartens, international and Russian schools nearby. The way from Nai Harn to the popular children's play complex "Rawai Park" will take 5 minutes by car or bike.

Nai Harn is also often chosen for yoga tours or sports campings. At Nai Harn and in the neighbouring Rawai district, there are gyms, specialised rings for Thai boxing and workout grounds. A 5-minute drive away is a hypermarket Makro, a supermarket with European products Villa Market, a fish market. The maximum number of schools and kindergartens is also concentrated in this area.

The complex is ideal for absolutely all categories of tourists. Ideal for families with children. The villas in the project are available for both short vacations and long term rentals. This project is often chosen by people who come to Phuket for the whole winter and expats for long term rentals. And also lovers of a calm and comfortable holiday on weekends.

4-Bedroom Villa, with garden view in Tamarind Villa project, on Chalong beach

Chalong is the practical and administrative heart of southern Phuket. It is not a beach destination in the traditional sense, since the bay is used as an anchorage for the islands rather than for swimming, but that is exactly why it works so well as a long stay base. Chalong Circle is the road junction where Phuket Town, Rawai, Kata and the Big Buddha all meet, which means almost everything the foreign community needs sits within a five kilometre radius: Makro, Tesco Lotus, Villa Market, half the islands visa agents, the immigration office, dental clinics, motorbike rentals and Mission Hospital. The expat population is large and mixed, with strong British, Australian, French, Scandinavian and Russian communities, plus a steady flow of families connected to the British Curriculum International School (BCIS), which sits right in the area. Day to day life skews residential. People live in moo baan estates and condos in the hills above the bay, drive to Rawai or Nai Harn for beach time, and use Chalong Pier for weekend trips to Coral Island, Racha and the Phi Phi group. Dining ranges from the long established Kan Eang at Pier on the bay to Greek Kitchen on the Big Buddha road and Chalong Bay Rum distillery tours. Chalong suits buyers who want infrastructure, school access and value rather than a beachfront address.

Chalong Circle with banks, Makro, Tesco Lotus and visa offices; Chalong Pier for island boats and seafood; Big Buddha access road; Villa Market in Chalong; Wat Chalong temple and surrounding local food strip; Friday Phuket Town night market 15 minutes north.

Mission Hospital Phuket (8 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (10 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (12 km, public, major trauma centre).

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Surin sits just south of Bang Tao on the same west coast strip, but the feel is noticeably more residential. The bay is a small crescent of yellow sand backed by a public park and a single row of low rise buildings, since the beach umbrellas and large clubs were cleared by the authorities a few years ago. What remained is a quieter beach that locals and long-term foreign residents actually use in the late afternoon. The Surin neighbourhood spreads up the hill behind the beach, full of mid-sized private villas, small condo projects and a steady population of European and Russian families who chose the area over Bang Tao precisely because it is calmer. Day to day life leans on Surin Plaza for groceries and basic services, with Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket reachable in under ten minutes by scooter. Schools are slightly further than from central Bang Tao but still inside a comfortable morning commute. The dining scene is small but well known, with Catch Beach Club at the Twinpalms resort just past the headland, plus Italian, Mediterranean and Thai seafood spots clustered along the main road. Healthcare is handled at Bangkok Hospital Phuket in town, around 30 minutes by car. Surin works best for people who want beach proximity, quieter nights and a residential feel.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (16 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (15 km, public, major trauma centre).

The unique project The Heights by renowned designer Hans Brouwer was built in 2009. Simple functional spaces and quality natural materials represent the best combination of east and west. The complex located on a hill offers a magnificent panoramic view of the Kata Bay, and in order to enjoy it to the fullest, the designer has created huge terraces with transparent railings. The project represents 51 residences, which are terraced one above the other on a hill, each of the residences has a separate entrance and a magnificent sea view. There are two types of residences in the project: 2-bedroom apartments with spacious terraces of 219m2 and duplex penthouses with 3 bedrooms, with private pools and the best sea views of 410m2. The project looks very modern, high ceilings, light colours, huge panoramic windows and straight lines. The Heights Phuket has won the Thailand Property Awards for Best Condominium in Thailand and Phuket.

The Heights offers its guests and owners the complete infrastructure of a good hotel: communal swimming pool, equipped fitness centre, sauna, covered parking. The complex is guarded round the clock and has a service company on the territory, which instantly solves all household issues of its residents and guests.

The huge advantage of the project over the rest is the stunning views of the sea and sunsets, plus its ideal location! Very close - in a straight line about 300 meters, along the road - a little further, but no more than 3-5 minutes by car, there are two beaches - the incredibly beautiful Kata Noi beach with the purest turquoise water and white sand, and the noisy, crowded Kata beach. In addition, the entire tourist infrastructure, everything you can wish for on holiday - massage, excursion bureaus, restaurants and cafés, bars, shops in a huge variety are within walking distance. Kata is one of the most popular tourist beaches, but there are no nightclubs and almost no bars, so it is quite calm at night. This area is often chosen for families. And if you go up the road from the apartment, then there you will find a viewpoint overlooking Kata Noi, Kata and Karon, and this road itself leads to Nai Harn Beach. The famous Mom Trees restaurant is located within walking distance.

The residences are very spacious and are ideal not only for relaxation, but also for long-term living. The Heights is chosen by those for whom look and space are very important, as well as lovers of modern style. Renting an apartment here will save you enormous money if you compare the cost of renting with living in hotels of a similar level.

Kata sits on the southwest coast, two bays south of Patong and one north of Nai Harn. The area is built around two beaches, Kata Yai and the smaller Kata Noi, both with cleaner sand and calmer water than Patong, plus a reliable surf break from May to October that keeps a small but committed long-stay surf community on the island year round. The foreign population here splits into three groups: surf and dive instructors who came on a season and stayed, retirees who chose Kata over Rawai for direct beach access, and remote workers who rent condos in Kata Hills for the views. Day to day life is walkable along Kata Beach Road and Patak Road, with bakeries, Thai kitchens, two small supermarkets and a steady rotation of cafes opening and closing each season. Nightlife is low key compared to Patong: a handful of bars, the Ska Bar sundowner spot under the banyan tree, and the weekend Kata Night Market for street food. Schools require a car, with Kajonkiet the closest international option and the Phuket Town cluster reachable in 25 to 30 minutes. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the Chalong side of the hill. The trade-offs are real high season traffic on the Patak hill road and limited supermarket options on site, but Kata works well for buyers who want a proper beach lifestyle without Patong density.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Layan is the northern continuation of Bang Tao Beach, separated by a small canal and a forested headland. The character changes immediately. Where Bang Tao has beach clubs and a busy main road, Layan is residential, low density and dominated by the Anantara Layan resort, a handful of branded villa estates and large private homes hidden behind walls in the hills. Foreign residents here tend to be at the higher end of the market and lean towards families with school-age children who want UWC or BISP within a ten minute drive but prefer not to live on top of Boat Avenue. The beach itself is short, shaded by casuarina trees, and has a fishing community at the canal mouth that keeps the atmosphere local rather than resort-styled. There are no large nightclubs and only a few restaurants directly on the sand, with the Beach House at Anantara as the main beachfront option. For daily errands most Layan residents drive south to Cherngtalay and Boat Avenue, which puts groceries, clinics, cafes and the Friday night market within four kilometres. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Bang Tao, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility in town. Layan suits buyers who want green surroundings, larger plots, beach access without crowds, and the lifestyle of the Cherngtalay corridor with one extra layer of quiet.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (16 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (15 km, public, major trauma centre).

Nikita Beach Restaurant (long established seafront spot under banyan trees), Reggae Bar Rawai, Friendship Beach (live music venue), Promthep Cape viewpoint dining, Rum Jungle Cafe (popular expat brunch spot on the way to Nai Harn).

Kamala fills the bay directly south of Surin, separated from it by a coastal headland that the locals call Laem Singh. The area has shifted character noticeably over the past five years. What used to be a quiet Muslim fishing village is now home to one of Asia top ranked beach clubs at Cafe del Mar, the Phuket International Academy school, and a steady stream of branded condo and villa launches in the hills behind the bay. The foreign community here is genuinely mixed: long term European retirees who arrived in the 1990s still live in older Kamala houses, while Russian, Chinese and Israeli families have moved into the newer hillside developments. The result is a place that feels less polished than Bang Tao but more residential than Patong. Daily life centres on the main road parallel to the beach, with a fresh market, small Thai restaurants, two minimarts, dive shops and an outsized number of property agents. The beach itself is a long, gentle arc of yellow sand that stays calm even in the green season inside the bay. Schools are well covered with PIA on the doorstep and Kajonkiet a short drive over the hill to Patong, while the Cherngtalay cluster sits ten minutes north. Healthcare follows the same pattern as Surin, with Bangkok Hospital Phuket the main private facility. Kamala suits buyers who want a real neighbourhood feel with strong beach club and dining options.

Kamala Beach Road with cafes and dive shops; Cafe del Mar Phuket area (beachfront events and dining); Plaza del Mar boutique mall; Kamala Fresh Market on the main road; Cherngtalay corridor reachable in 10 minutes north.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai sits at the southern tip of Phuket and has the longest established foreign resident community on the island. People started settling here in the 1990s for two reasons: cheap land back then, and a coastline that faces calm water on the east side rather than the surf of the west coast. The result is a town that feels lived in rather than touristic. The main road runs parallel to the seafront and is full of long-stay infrastructure: international clinics, dental practices, scuba schools, yoga studios, two large supermarkets, dozens of small Thai restaurants and a steady rotation of European-run cafes and bakeries. The demographic skews older than Bang Tao, with a heavy Scandinavian, German, French and Russian presence, plus a growing number of families who chose Rawai specifically for the lower density and direct access to the southern beaches. Day to day, Nai Harn beach is five minutes west, Promthep Cape ten, and Chalong Pier ten minutes north for boats to the islands. The trade-off is that Rawai is roughly 40 minutes from the airport and 25 minutes from Patong, so it works best for people whose life is rooted on the south end of the island. Schools require a car ride into Phuket Town. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket. Rawai is the practical choice for long-stay residents who value community over beachfront glamour.

Rawai Beach Road and seafront promenade with seafood market and Sea Gypsy village; Rawai weekly markets (Tuesday and Friday) for street food and produce; Nai Harn Beach area (5 minutes drive west); Chalong Circle (5 km north) for Makro, banks and visa runs.

Mission Hospital Phuket (12 km, private); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (16 km, JCI-accredited); Vachira Phuket Hospital (15 km, public, major trauma centre).

Nikita Beach Restaurant (long established seafront spot under banyan trees), Reggae Bar Rawai, Friendship Beach (live music venue), Promthep Cape viewpoint dining, Rum Jungle Cafe (popular expat brunch spot on the way to Nai Harn).

The Title Nai Yang is a modern resort complex, which consists of seven buildings of 6 and 7 floors and has 472 apartments: studios 36-39m2, one-bedroom apartments with an area of ​​46m2 or two bedrooms, the territory of the complex itself is fenced and is under 24-hour video surveillance and security ... The concept of the project and design is somewhat unusual for Thailand, the complex is decorated with red brick, and it looks more like a medieval castle than a modern Asian condominium. The apartments have a comfortable layout, in light grey and blue colours. The common area is a beautiful, well-groomed recreation park, a river flows along the buildings, which gives the project a certain charm and beauty of the fusion of modern urban architecture with nature.

The complex has its own restaurant, which serves breakfast, lunch and dinner a-la carte. Each building has access to a communal pool and well-kept garden. 5 swimming pools in each building are located on the 1st floor, and the sixth is on the roof of one of the buildings. There is a recreation area on the same roof. The complex offers a free gym, two saunas, a reception, a play area for children in the form of a pirate ship. Parking for 240 cars is organized on the south side of the building and is separated by green spaces and a fence.

The complex blends in perfectly with the tropical environment, and walking to the beach is a real pleasure. Just 5 minutes, and you will find yourself on one of the most stunning beaches in Phuket - Nai Yang. A small, cosy beach with a length of just under 3 kilometres, the water area of ​​which is protected by coral reefs, will allow you to enjoy swimming in the sea all year round, regardless of the season. Since 1986, this beach has been part of the Sirinath National Park Marine Park and all motor sports are prohibited on it. There is a large selection of restaurants, bars and cafés along the beach. The Title project itself separates the famous 5 * hotel The Slate from the beach with excellent gourmet restaurants. A five-minute walk is a local grocery market and mini markets.

The proximity to the sea and low prices make this project one of the most attractive on the island. And the peculiarity of the Nai Yang beach, on which there are never waves, even in low season, makes the project popular all year round. The entrance to the water is very shallow, so the beach is loved by families with small children. The low cost of apartments, both for rent and for purchase, makes the project accessible to everyone.

Nai Yang sits inside Sirinat National Park, just south of Mai Khao and a few minutes north of the airport. The bay is a long shallow arc with calm water in the dry season and proper Andaman swell in green season, which makes it one of the few west coast spots where local surfers actually gather. The village strip is small but real: a row of seafood restaurants facing the beach under the casuarina trees, a few dive shops, two yoga studios, a daily night market that sets up on the inland road and a small cluster of guesthouses. That mix gives Nai Yang a character that Mai Khao lacks. There is a village to walk to in the evening, a community of long-stay foreign residents who actually use it, and prices for both rentals and groceries are noticeably softer than down at Bang Tao. The resident expat profile leans toward families, retirees and remote workers who decided that proximity to the airport and a quieter beach mattered more than walking distance to Boat Avenue. Schools are 20 to 25 minutes south, hospitals are 30 minutes, and a car or scooter is essential. The Slate and Marriott resorts anchor the upper end of the dining scene, and the Carpe Diem and Coco Beach groups handle casual sunset crowds. Nai Yang rewards buyers who want a village feel without leaving the west coast.

Nai Yang village strip with seafood restaurants and beachfront cafes; Nai Yang night market (Thursdays and weekends) for cheap Thai food; The Slate resort dining hub; Boat Avenue and Porto de Phuket (about 18 km, 20 minutes south) for chain grocery and international restaurants; airport area Makro for bulk shopping.

Thalang Hospital — public (7 km); Bangkok Hospital Phuket (30 km); Mission Hospital Phuket (33 km). No large private hospital in the immediate north; expats typically register with Bangkok Hospital Phuket.

Patong is the loudest part of Phuket and also the most misunderstood by long-stay buyers. Yes, Bangla Road and the beer bars define the tourist image, but the actual expat population in Patong is sizeable and quite different from the visitors. Many are restaurant and bar owners, dive instructors, hospitality staff, long-term Russian and Indian families, and remote workers who simply prefer walkable density to a quiet villa estate. Patong is the only part of Phuket where you can genuinely live without a car, with supermarkets, gyms, clinics, the public hospital and the beach all reachable on foot from most condo blocks. Daytime is calm: the three kilometre beach is busy but functional, surf is decent in green season, and the back sois fill with cafes, laundries and family-run Thai kitchens. The party belt occupies roughly six streets and is easy to avoid. Bangkok Hospital Phuket is about 20 minutes over the hill through Patong Bypass tunnel access, which opened up the commute considerably. School-age families usually choose Kajonkiet or QSI nearby, or accept a longer drive to BISP. The main trade-offs are noise in the central blocks, high-season traffic on the hill roads, and a rental market that swings sharply between November and April peaks and the quieter monsoon months.

Kata sits on the southwest coast, two bays south of Patong and one north of Nai Harn. The area is built around two beaches, Kata Yai and the smaller Kata Noi, both with cleaner sand and calmer water than Patong, plus a reliable surf break from May to October that keeps a small but committed long-stay surf community on the island year round. The foreign population here splits into three groups: surf and dive instructors who came on a season and stayed, retirees who chose Kata over Rawai for direct beach access, and remote workers who rent condos in Kata Hills for the views. Day to day life is walkable along Kata Beach Road and Patak Road, with bakeries, Thai kitchens, two small supermarkets and a steady rotation of cafes opening and closing each season. Nightlife is low key compared to Patong: a handful of bars, the Ska Bar sundowner spot under the banyan tree, and the weekend Kata Night Market for street food. Schools require a car, with Kajonkiet the closest international option and the Phuket Town cluster reachable in 25 to 30 minutes. Healthcare is well covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the Chalong side of the hill. The trade-offs are real high season traffic on the Patak hill road and limited supermarket options on site, but Kata works well for buyers who want a proper beach lifestyle without Patong density.

Kata Beach Road with cafes, dive shops and surf rentals; Kata Night Market (weekends) on Patak Road; Karon Plaza shopping strip (3 km north); Big C and Tesco Lotus in Chalong (10 km east) for full grocery runs.

Nai Harn is the bay immediately west of Rawai and consistently ranks among the best swimming beaches on Phuket. The water inside the bay is calm and clear for most of the year and the sand is wider and cleaner than the more developed beaches further north. The neighbourhood itself stays surprisingly residential because most of the land directly behind the beach belongs to a Buddhist monastery and a freshwater lagoon, which capped large scale resort development. Foreign residents here lean towards families and retirees who want beach access without the foot traffic of Patong or Kata. The Nai Harn and Wyndham Grand are the two main resort anchors, but daily life happens in the small grid of streets behind the lagoon where you find German Bakery, Amalfi Italian, Banana Corner, Cosmo and a steady rotation of yoga studios and gyms. Rawai is five minutes east for fresh seafood at the Sea Gypsy village and for the weekly markets. Schools require a 20 to 25 minute drive into Phuket Town, which is the main practical compromise for families. Healthcare is covered by Mission Hospital and Bangkok Hospital Phuket on the same Chalong side of the island. Nai Harn suits buyers who specifically want a swimmable beach, low density living and a quieter community feel than Kata or Patong.
